rationale: B wins because it finds the live business-model story A wrongly threw in the trash. A says "Business/revenue mechanics" has "no_journalist_shape" because "No revenue terms disclosed"; that is exactly the reporter's opening when the same update gives you 4 million paid subscribers and 25 million no-cost eligible members. B's "Calm has 4 million paying subscribers. Its insurer deal hands the app free to 25 million." turns the hole into a sharp question without pretending to know the answer.
gaps_in_A: "Business/revenue mechanics" / "No revenue terms disclosed" is a bad refusal. Undisclosed terms plus 4 million paid subscribers and 25 million no-cost covered members is a real business-model angle, not a reason to kill it.
"The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" overstates the facts. The update supports payer coverage plus a peer-reviewed study, not a declared category migration into clinical care.
"Coverage Was the Last Wall" is too cute and too broad. Coverage is not the last wall if insurer names, plan types, activation steps, uptake, and outcomes are all still missing.

"The countervailing evidence - from pharmaceutical research, food science, and now digital health" imports a larger funder-effect argument not supplied in the update. It may be a valid reporting path, but A sells it harder than its evidence allows.
gaps_in_B: "pointing to a randomized trial as the reason" implies payer causality the update does not prove. Keep it as a question insurers must answer, not as stated motive.

"Your health plan may now include Calm Premium at no cost. Here is how to check." is only pitchable after the insurers and activation steps are public. B admits that, but the headline still gets ahead of the available facts.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the strongest business angle. This is subscription economics, payer revenue structure, and cannibalization risk, not funding mechanics.
